what_it_does.text: Temporarily raises the cap on deducting state and local taxes from $10,000 to $40,000 for 2025, with 1% yearly growth through 2029, then returns it to $10,000 in 2030. The increase is smaller for filers with income above $500,000.

Makes the 2017-era lower income tax rates and the larger standard deduction permanent, and raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child. Filers who itemize get little added benefit from the standard deduction change.

Trims the value of itemized deductions, including state and local taxes, mortgage interest and charity, for filers in the top 37% bracket. It also keeps the $750,000 mortgage interest cap, adds a 0.5%-of-income floor on charitable deductions for itemizers, and makes the higher alternative minimum tax exemption permanent while phasing it out faster for very high earners.
Adds temporary deductions through 2028 for seniors, tips, overtime and new U.S.-assembled car loan interest, each of which shrinks as income rises.

Changes Medicaid funding and eligibility rules for expansion states like New Jersey. It caps extra hospital payments and provider taxes, adds work requirements and six-month renewals, shortens back-coverage, and ends federal matching funds for many lawfully present immigrants.

Ends several clean energy tax credits, including those for home solar, home energy upgrades, and new wind and solar projects. It also expands business tax breaks such as full equipment expensing and immediate deduction of U.S. research costs.

overview.district_bottom_line: For this high-income, high-property-tax suburban district, the larger SALT cap and permanent lower rates are the most direct household tax items among the provisions reviewed. The SALT increase shrinks above $500,000 of income, top-bracket itemizers lose part of their deductions, and the Medicaid changes could strain New Jersey's budget and local hospitals, though the text does not say by how much.

items.headline: Makes 2017-era lower income tax rates permanent for district taxpayers
items.plain_english: The lower individual income tax rates set in 2017 were due to expire after 2025. This section removes that end date, so the rates continue for tax years starting in 2026 and later, and families avoid the scheduled rate increase. It also makes a technical change to how some tax brackets are adjusted for inflation.
items.who_in_district: Most households in this high-income, mostly white-collar district would keep the current rate structure, including the many middle- and upper-income families in management and professional jobs.

items.headline: Caps extra Medicaid payments to hospitals, shrinking them over time
items.plain_english: Some states pay hospitals and other providers extra Medicaid money on top of regular rates. This section caps those payments at 100% of the Medicare rate in states that have expanded Medicaid, which includes New Jersey. Non-expansion states get a higher 110% cap. Existing payments are grandfathered at first, then cut by 10 percentage points each year starting in 2028 until they reach the cap, which could reduce what local hospitals and nursing homes receive for Medicaid patients.

items.headline: Caps state Medicaid provider taxes and lowers the limit for New Jersey from 2028
items.plain_english: New Jersey is an expansion state, so it could not add new provider taxes. Its existing taxes would be held at current levels, and the allowed ceiling would fall from 5.5% of net patient revenue in 2028 to 3.5% by 2032. Taxes on nursing homes and similar facilities are kept at their current levels rather than stepped down. Whether the state or its hospitals lose money depends on how far above the ceiling its taxes sit, and the bill text does not say.

items.headline: Child tax credit made permanent and raised to $2,200 per child
items.plain_english: The larger child tax credit would no longer expire after 2025. It rises from $2,000 to $2,200 per child and is adjusted for inflation after 2025. Parents must now give a Social Security number for themselves (at least one spouse on a joint return) and for each child, and the child's number must be issued to a U.S. citizen or under certain work-authorized categories.

items.headline: Companies can again deduct U.S. research costs immediately, which suits the district's professional economy
items.plain_english: The section lets businesses deduct U.S.-based research and software development costs in the year they are spent, instead of spreading them over five years. Foreign research stays on a 15-year schedule. Small businesses can apply the change back to 2022, and all firms can deduct leftover amounts from 2022–2024 research. The section doesn't touch SALT or Medicaid.

items.plain_english: The bill removes the 2025 end date on the current mortgage interest limit, so the lower cap stays in place rather than reverting to the older, higher one. It also keeps mortgage insurance premiums treated as deductible interest. Homeowners with larger mortgages gain no relief from the cap, while those with low down payments keep a deduction.

items.plain_english: This section cuts off the 30 percent federal tax credit for homeowners' clean energy upgrades, such as rooftop solar, for any spending after December 31, 2025. It had been set to run through 2034, so the cut removes years of expected savings. Households that wanted to install systems later will pay full price.

items.headline: Adds a temporary $6,000 senior deduction; keeps the personal exemption at zero
items.plain_english: Through 2028, each taxpayer 65 or older can deduct $6,000, or $12,000 for a couple where both qualify. The deduction shrinks by 6 cents for every dollar of income above $75,000 for single filers or $150,000 for joint filers, so it disappears entirely $100,000 above those lines. The section also ends the old per-person personal exemption for good, so it never returns after 2025. Seniors and each qualifying person need a Social Security number on the return.

items.plain_english: Starting in 2027, adults 19-64 covered through Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, service, or school, or equivalent income. Many are exempt, including parents of children 13 and under, people with disabilities, and the medically frail. Others who can't show compliance after a 30-day notice lose coverage, though states get $200 million in grants to build verification systems.

items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, this raises the share of child and dependent care costs that families can claim as a tax credit. The top rate goes from 35% to 50%. Families keep at least 35% until income passes $75,000 ($150,000 for joint filers), then the rate phases down to a 20% floor. Joint filers near this district's median income would stay in the higher-rate range, while higher earners see little change.

items.plain_english: Wind and solar projects that start construction after a date about a year after enactment, and are placed in service after 2027, lose the clean electricity production credit. All remaining projects face new limits on Chinese and other foreign-linked equipment and ownership, backed by tougher penalties. Nuclear projects get easier access to a bonus credit. items.plain_english: This section ends a federal tax credit for wind and solar power projects placed in service after 2027, though battery storage at those sites is exempt. It also denies the credit for leased home solar and wind equipment, and adds limits on foreign-linked companies. Fuel cells get a 30 percent credit under the section. items.headline: Limits state Medicaid provider taxes that charge Medicaid-heavy providers more
items.plain_english: The section bars states from taxing hospitals, nursing homes, or other providers at higher rates because they serve more Medicaid patients, or from taxing Medicaid business more heavily than non-Medicaid business. Taxes like that would no longer count as acceptable for federal Medicaid matching purposes. States may get up to 3 fiscal years to adjust. The section doesn't say how New Jersey's taxes would be affected, so any effect on local hospitals and nursing homes depends on how the state's current taxes are built.

items.plain_english: The section blocks the federal government from putting into effect parts of a 2024 rule that made it easier to apply for and stay enrolled in Medicaid, CHIP, and the Basic Health Program. These parts stay on hold until September 30, 2034. Fewer eligible people may be enrolled, and the paperwork burden on states stays as it is.

items.plain_english: Today Medicaid can pay for care received up to three months before someone applies. For applications made after 2026, that drops to one month for people covered under the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion and two months for everyone else, with a two-month limit for CHIP too. Residents who sign up late, such as after a sudden illness or hospital stay, could be left with bills Medicaid would once have paid. Hospitals and nursing homes could also absorb more unpaid care.

items.headline: Marketplace enrollees must verify eligibility before getting premium tax credits
items.plain_english: Starting in 2028, people buying marketplace health plans would get premium tax credits only for months after the exchange verifies their income, family size, immigration status, other coverage, and residence. Months before verification can still count if the applicant verifies them later. The bill also requires exchanges to offer a pre-enrollment verification process by August 1. This could screen out ineligible claims, but it adds paperwork and could delay or interrupt help for eligible people.
items.who_in_district: Marketplace enrollees in this relatively affluent district, which has a low poverty rate and few Medicaid recipients, would face new verification steps, with the most exposure among self-employed, gig, and lower-income workers who buy their own coverage.

items.plain_english: Starting October 1, 2026, the federal government would pay a state for Medicaid or CHIP only for U.S. citizens, green card holders, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and residents covered by Compact of Free Association agreements. Lawfully present immigrants in other categories, such as refugees and asylees, would lose federal matching funds. New Jersey would either have to cover them with its own money or drop their coverage. It also guarantees at least a $400 deduction for owners who actively work in a business earning $1,000 or more. Higher-earning owners and very small active business owners both come out ahead.

items.plain_english: Workers can deduct the overtime premium (the extra half-time portion) they earn, up to $12,500 ($25,000 for joint filers), from 2025 through 2028. The deduction shrinks for incomes above $150,000 ($300,000 joint) and requires a Social Security number and joint filing for married couples. items.headline: Keeps higher AMT exemptions but speeds up phase-out for top earners
items.plain_english: The alternative minimum tax is a parallel tax calculation that can catch higher earners. This section makes the larger exemption permanent instead of letting it expire after 2025. That likely keeps most upper-middle-income families out of the AMT. It also makes the exemption shrink at 50 percent instead of 25 percent for very high earners, with the phase-out starting at $1,000,000 (indexed from 2025), so the biggest earners lose more of the exemption.
items.who_in_district: Most affected are well-off homeowners, especially those with large property tax bills who could otherwise be exposed to the AMT, while households with very high incomes lose part of the exemption sooner.

items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, people who itemize can deduct charitable gifts only to the extent they exceed 0.5 percent of their contribution base (roughly their income). Gifts under that threshold produce no tax benefit, though the disallowed amount can be carried forward to later years. This raises the after-tax cost of giving for itemizers.

items.plain_english: The section ends the federal tax credit for energy-efficient home improvements for items placed in service after December 31, 2025. Under current law the credit would have run through 2032. Homeowners in the district who plan upgrades after 2025 would lose that tax break. The second part is a technical edit to the oil furnace and boiler rules.

items.plain_english: From 2025 through 2028, workers can deduct up to $25,000 a year in cash tips from taxable income, whether or not they itemize. The deduction shrinks for individuals earning over $150,000 ($300,000 on a joint return) and requires a Social Security number and a joint return for married couples. The bill also extends an employer tip credit to hair, nail, esthetics and spa businesses, and adds new tip-reporting duties for employers and payers.

items.plain_english: Families can use 529 accounts tax-free for more K-12 costs: curriculum, books, online materials, outside tutoring, test fees, dual enrollment, and therapies for students with disabilities. items.headline: One-year Medicaid payment ban on certain abortion-providing family planning clinics
items.plain_english: For one year after enactment, Medicaid cannot pay certain nonprofit family planning and reproductive health providers that offer abortions beyond the rape, incest and life-endangering exceptions. The ban applies to providers that received more than $800,000 in Medicaid payments in fiscal year 2023. The section does not name any provider, and it gives no data on whether any are in the district. Medicaid patients who use a covered provider would have to go elsewhere for that care, or the provider would have to cover the loss.

items.headline: Medicaid waivers must be cost-neutral to Washington starting 2027
items.plain_english: Starting in 2027, CMS can approve, renew, or change a state's Medicaid waiver project only if its chief actuary certifies the project won't raise federal spending. Spending on services a state could already cover under its regular Medicaid plan counts as the baseline, which makes it harder for a waiver to clear the test. Waivers that fail could be blocked or scaled back, while any savings a state achieves would be taken into account in the next approval period.
items.who_in_district: The roughly 41,192 residents on Medicaid or similar coverage, and the hospitals and providers serving them, would be affected only if New Jersey's waiver programs can't meet the cost-neutrality test.

items.headline: Trims the value of itemized deductions for top-bracket filers only
items.plain_english: Taxpayers in the highest (37%) income bracket would lose part of the tax benefit from deductions such as state and local taxes, mortgage interest and charity. The reduction is 2/37 of the deductions, or of the income above the start of that bracket if that is smaller. Filers below that bracket are not touched.

items.headline: Payment apps report only larger sellers to the IRS again
items.plain_english: This section restores the older rule that payment apps and online marketplaces report a seller's earnings to the IRS only above $20,000 and more than 200 transactions. Casual sellers and side-gig earners below those levels would get fewer tax forms and less paperwork, and backup withholding would follow the same thresholds. The income is still taxable, but the IRS would see less of it automatically.
items.who_in_district: Residents who sell online, do occasional gig work, or work from home would benefit most from less paperwork, while the change matters little to the large share of salaried professionals.

items.headline: Storm and fire losses stay deductible, now including state-declared disasters
items.plain_english: Under current law, individuals can deduct uninsured losses from disasters only if the federal government declares them, and that rule was set to expire after 2025. This section makes the rule permanent and also covers disasters that the Governor and the Treasury Secretary agree are severe enough, even without a federal declaration. A New Jersey family hit by a flood, storm or fire could claim a deduction in more cases.
items.who_in_district: Homeowners in the district, about 76.4% of homes, who suffer uninsured storm, flood or fire damage in a year with a state-declared disaster but no federal declaration.

items.headline: Car loan interest deduction helps many NJ-7 households buying new U.S.-assembled cars
items.plain_english: For 2025 through 2028, buyers can deduct up to $10,000 a year in interest on a loan for a new personal vehicle that was assembled in the U.S., even if they don't itemize. The deduction shrinks by $200 for every $1,000 of income over $100,000 ($200,000 for joint filers) and disappears at high incomes. Used cars, leases, and vehicles assembled abroad don't qualify, and lenders must report the interest.
items.who_in_district: Middle- and upper-middle-income households in the district who finance a new U.S.-assembled vehicle benefit most, while higher earners lose part or all of the deduction and used-car or foreign-assembled buyers get nothing.

items.headline: New child investment accounts with $1,000 federal seed for births 2025-2028
items.plain_english: The section creates tax-advantaged investment accounts for children under 18. Families can put in up to $5,000 a year, and employers can add up to $2,500 tax-free. Children born from 2025 through 2028 who are U.S. citizens with a Social Security number can get a $1,000 federal deposit. Money is locked until the year the child turns 18 and must go into low-cost U.S. stock index funds. Families with spare cash and employer participation gain the most.
items.who_in_district: Higher-income, mostly owner-occupied households with young children and professional employers (55.3% in management/professional jobs) are best placed to use the accounts, while the 5.2% of residents below poverty are less likely to have money to add.

items.headline: Lets indebted businesses deduct more interest; RV dealers get added relief
items.plain_english: Starting with tax years that begin after 2024, the section sets the cap on business interest deductions so that it is figured on income before depreciation and amortization. That usually raises the cap, so companies with significant debt can deduct more interest. It also lets dealers of towable campers and trailers count their inventory loan interest under the special floor plan financing rule.
items.who_in_district: The benefit goes to owners of debt-financed or equipment-heavy businesses, such as contractors, manufacturers, and vehicle or RV dealers, rather than to typical wage earners.

items.headline: Full first-year write-off for new factory buildings, with limited local reach
items.plain_english: The section lets manufacturers deduct the full cost of new factory buildings, including those for agricultural or chemical production, in the year the building is first used. This applies only to construction that starts between January 20, 2025 and the end of 2028, and the building must be in use by 2031. Offices, research space, parking, and sales areas are excluded, and landlords cannot claim it for buildings leased to others. The deduction is recaptured if the building is switched to another use within 10 years.
items.who_in_district: Manufacturers and other production businesses that build or buy new plant space would benefit, but only 7.5% of district workers are in production and transportation jobs, and most work in management, business, science and arts (55.3%).

items.plain_english: The section removes the credit's expiration date and widens it. Employers could claim it on insurance premiums as well as wages paid during leave, and employees would qualify after 6 months on the job instead of a year. Leave that a state or local government pays for or requires does not count toward the credit, so employers in states with their own leave mandates may get less from it.
items.who_in_district: Employers in the district, and the roughly 55% of workers in management, business, science and arts jobs plus the sales, office and service workforce, could see more employer-offered leave, while much of the benefit may be offset where state law already covers leave.

items.headline: Bigger tax credit for employers who provide child care
items.plain_english: The bill raises the federal credit for employers that pay for child care for their workers. It goes from 25% to 40% of qualifying costs, or 50% for small businesses, and the cap rises to $500,000, or $600,000 for small businesses. It also lets employers get the credit when they use a middleman to arrange care or share a facility with others. These changes apply to spending after December 31, 2025.
items.who_in_district: Working parents and employers in a district where 55.3% of workers are in management, business, science and arts jobs and 15.7% work from home, though only employers that choose to fund child care would use the credit.

items.headline: Changes how big companies' foreign profits are taxed; little direct local effect
items.plain_english: This section renames the minimum tax on foreign subsidiaries' profits and ends the rule that exempted a set return on their physical assets abroad. It also renames the export-income deduction and removes the old asset-based wording from it. Companies that keep factories and equipment overseas could owe more, and the section does not give rates or dollar amounts. The changes start with tax years after December 31, 2025.

items.plain_english: Employers can keep paying up to $5,250 a year toward an employee's student loans without it counting as taxable income. That break was set to end for payments after 2025, and this makes it permanent. From 2027 on, the $5,250 limit rises with inflation.
items.who_in_district: Workers with student loans at employers that offer repayment help, especially the large share of professional and managerial workers in this high-income, well-educated district.

items.plain_english: This section makes the opportunity zone program permanent. It re-picks eligible low-income census tracts every 10 years, starting in 2026, and offers investors a capital gains tax deferral with larger breaks for rural funds. It also adds new reporting rules and public data reports. NJ-7 is a high-income suburban district, so it likely has few qualifying tracts. Any benefit would come from investment in those tracts, and the tighter eligibility test and rural bonus mostly point elsewhere.
items.who_in_district: Residents of any low-income tracts in the district and investors who put capital gains into opportunity funds could be affected, but most of the district's households are well above the income cutoffs.

items.headline: Bigger, faster tax break for selling small-company stock favors few residents
items.plain_english: The section lets investors in qualifying small companies exclude part of their profit from tax after 3 years instead of 5. It also raises the cap on excluded gain per company from $10 million to $15 million and lifts the company asset limit from $50 million to $75 million. The benefit goes mainly to founders, early employees and investors who sell stock at a large gain.
items.who_in_district: Founders, startup employees and investors in this high-income, management-heavy district (median household income $132,702; 55.3% of workers in management, business, science and arts) could gain, while most residents would see no direct change.

items.plain_english: The section moves the end date of the tax credit for businesses that buy qualifying clean commercial vehicles from the end of 2032 to September 30, 2025. Local businesses and fleets that planned to buy electric vans or trucks after that date would lose the credit, which makes those vehicles more expensive to buy. The section does not touch household taxes or benefits, so the effect is limited to businesses that buy these vehicles.
items.who_in_district: Small businesses, contractors, delivery and trucking operators, and other fleet owners in the district's construction, maintenance, production and transportation trades would be most affected.

items.plain_english: The section removes the quick five-year depreciation schedule that clean electricity projects could use. It applies to projects that begin construction after December 31, 2024. Developers would write off costs more slowly, which can make new projects costlier to build and could eventually raise power costs. The effect on this district is indirect.
items.who_in_district: The most exposed are construction and maintenance workers and local businesses that build or buy solar, storage, or other clean power projects, while homeowners are mostly unaffected directly.

items.headline: Permanent cap on business losses trims write-offs for some owners
items.plain_english: Business owners who file as individuals, such as sole proprietors, partners, and S-corporation owners, can only use a limited amount of business losses against other income, like wages or investment gains. This section removes the 2028 expiration, so the limit becomes permanent. It also resets the starting year for the yearly inflation adjustment, so the limit grows from a newer base and may be lower than under current law. Owners with large losses would pay more tax sooner.
items.who_in_district: The people most affected are higher-income owners of pass-through businesses, professional practices, and real estate or investment ventures, and only those with large business losses, in a district where 55.3% of workers are in management, business, science and arts jobs.

items.plain_english: The section fines paid preparers who promote the COVID employee retention credit without checking eligibility, at $1,000 per failure. It also bars any new credit claims filed after January 31, 2024, and gives the IRS six years to audit claims. Employers with legitimate claims already on file are unaffected, but anyone who hasn't filed loses the chance.
items.who_in_district: Small and mid-sized employers in the district that claimed or planned to claim the credit, and the tax and payroll firms that advised them, are most directly affected, in a district where 55.3% of workers are in management, business, science and arts jobs.

items.plain_english: Starting October 1, 2026, the federal government would pay no more than the state's regular Medicaid share for emergency care given to certain non-citizens. Citizens' benefits do not change directly, but New Jersey may have to cover more of these costs or pass them on to hospitals.

items.plain_english: This section changes how multinational companies divide their deductions between U.S. and foreign income when they figure the foreign tax credit. items.plain_english: Businesses would only have to send tax forms (like 1099s) to contractors and others they pay once payments reach more than $2,000 a year, up from $600. The threshold would rise with inflation after 2026. Small businesses and freelancers would have less paperwork, but fewer small payments would be reported to the IRS.

items.headline: 1% tax on cash remittances; bank-funded transfers exempt
items.plain_english: Starting in 2026, anyone sending money abroad using cash, a money order, or a cashier's check pays a 1% tax, collected by the transfer company. Transfers paid from a bank account or with a U.S.-issued debit or credit card are exempt. Because most of the district's households are higher-income and likely use bank-linked methods, few residents would be affected, but cash senders would pay more.
items.who_in_district: Cash-based senders, such as immigrant families in the district's Hispanic (14.0%) and Asian (8.9%) communities who wire money abroad, would pay the 1% tax, while most residents using bank accounts or cards would not.

items.plain_english: Starting in 2027, states must regularly check enrollees' addresses against sources like the Postal Service change-of-address list and health plan records. By October 2029, states must also use a new federal system to catch people enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP in more than one state, and drop them from a state where they no longer live. Most people are unaffected, though anyone who moves out of state without updating their address could lose coverage in the old state.
items.who_in_district: The roughly 41,192 residents on Medicaid or other means-tested coverage could be affected, mainly those who recently moved or whose address records are out of date, but most should see no change.

promise_alerts.explanation: The commitment has two parts: protecting Medicaid for "every intended beneficiary" and stopping illegal immigrants from getting benefits. The bill partly meets the second part, since people here illegally are already barred from Medicaid and it adds checks such as duplicate-enrollment checks and marketplace eligibility verification. On the first part, it adds work requirements, six-month renewals for expansion adults, a shorter back-coverage window, provider payment caps, and a pause on enrollment-simplification rules, and these could cut coverage for eligible people. Whether that contradicts "protected Medicaid for every intended beneficiary" depends on how "intended beneficiary" is read, and the statement was also about the House-passed version rather than this text.

The commitment says the most vulnerable should never lose care because of waste, fraud, or abuse. H.R. 1 pairs anti-fraud measures, such as duplicate-enrollment checks, eligibility-error penalties, and marketplace verification, with changes that could cost eligible people coverage. These include 80-hour work requirements, six-month renewals, a shorter back-coverage window, and a pause on enrollment-simplification rules. Whether this conflicts depends on how "vulnerable" and "because of fraud" are read, since many losses would come from paperwork and eligibility rules rather than a finding of fraud. The commitment was also made after the bill became law and does not name a specific vote.

The commitment says the member voted to protect New Jersey's expansion of supplemental Medicaid payments to hospitals and nursing homes. The bill partly fits this: existing payments are grandfathered at first (71116), and nursing-home provider taxes are held at current levels rather than stepped down (71115). But the bill also bars new provider taxes in expansion states like New Jersey, lowers the provider-tax ceiling from 2028, and cuts grandfathered payments by 10 percentage points a year from 2028 toward the 100% Medicare cap. Whether this contradicts the commitment depends on which payments he meant and whether New Jersey's expansion falls inside the grandfathering, which the findings do not say.

The commitment is a general campaign message (lower the cost of living, protect healthcare, strengthen communities, keep America strong), not a specific pledge on a vote or provision. The bill cuts both ways. It raises the SALT cap, makes the child tax credit and lower tax rates permanent, and expands child-care credits. It also caps Medicaid provider payments and taxes, adds work requirements and six-month renewals, cuts federal funds for some lawfully present immigrants, and ends home energy credits. Whether a YES vote conflicts with 'protect healthcare' and 'lower the cost of living' depends on how those broad phrases are read.
